1. The interpretive history of the "sons of God" (bnei elohim) in Genesis 6 is among the strangest in the reception history of the Bible.
2. The Book of Enoch is an ancient Jewish work.
3. The Book of Enoch is preserved most fully in Ethiopic versions.
4. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church reads the Book of Enoch as scripture.
5. The Book of Enoch elaborated a tradition of fallen angels called the Watchers.
6. In the Book of Enoch, the Watchers descended to corrupt humanity.
7. In the Book of Enoch, the Watchers corrupted humanity through forbidden teaching.
8. In the Book of Enoch, the Watchers corrupted humanity through miscegenation.
9. Jude 6 may presuppose the fallen-angel reading of the sons of God.
10. 2 Peter 2:4 may presuppose the fallen-angel reading of the sons of God.
11. Augustine, in City of God, rejected the angelic interpretation of the sons of God.
12. Augustine favored the Sethite interpretation of Genesis 6.
13. In the Sethite interpretation, the sons of God are the godly line of Seth.
14. In the Sethite interpretation, the daughters of men are the line of Cain.
15. Readers have compared the Genesis 6 passage with ancient Near Eastern traditions.
16. In some ancient Near Eastern traditions, kings and other powerful men claimed descent from gods.
17. Genesis 6 introduces the flood narrative.
18. The biblical flood narrative belongs to a broader Mesopotamian flood tradition.
19. The Mesopotamian flood tradition is preserved most fully in the Atrahasis epic and in tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh.
20. Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh contains the Utnapishtim narrative.
21. The Atrahasis epic and tablet XI of Gilgamesh contain close parallels to the biblical flood story.
22. The Hebrew word for the vessel Noah builds is tevah.
23. Tevah means "ark" or "chest."
24. Outside the Noah story, Scripture uses tevah only for the basket in which the infant Moses is set adrift on the Nile.
